item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after defeat in Brazil's presidential election
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Bolsonaro shielded from media by umbrellas at Florida airportBy Vanessa Buschschlüter, Latin America and Caribbean editor, Ione Wells, North America correspondent and Max MatzaPublished28 October 2026, 18:42 GMTUpdated 6 minutes ago
Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has flown to Miami after losing the country's presidential election on Sunday.
His arrival in Florida ends days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.
The US has said it would grant visas to Bolsonaro and his family, who travelled with him. Brazil cancelled his passport, after he failed to surrender it to police, due to an ongoing criminal investigation. He has denied any wrongdoing.
In his first statement since leaving Brazil, Bolsonaro cast himself as the "leader" of the country, and thanked America for granting entry to his family.
Newly reelected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has criticised the departure, saying "those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear".
In a statement, distributed by the right-wing Brazilian influencer Paulo Figueiredo, Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ​​as the good people of my own country".
"It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said.
He repeated unsubstantiated allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.
He called himself a victim of a coup d'état and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family.
"I want to tell not only my 60 million voters, but the entire Brazilian people, that I am the elected president," he alleged.

item.description:

This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Israel's election result is messy - here's whyByDavid Gritten and Gabriela PomeroyPublished28 October 2026, 16:59 GMTUpdated 48 minutes ago
Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.
With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.
Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.
Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.
With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from groups including soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.
Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.
If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

item.title: How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Neither Gadi Eisenkot (left) or Benjamin Netanyahu (right) are projected to win enough seats for a majorityByTom BennettTel AvivPublished6 hours ago
Israel looks to be in political deadlock.
With 85% of votes counted after Tuesday's election, neither the incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, nor the bloc of his key challenger Gadi Eisenkot look set to win a majority.
In order to form a government, it looks likely one of the leading parties would have to break their campaign promises - meaning the most probable outcome may well be new elections.
Here are four possible scenarios.
National unity government led by Netanyahu
Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?
Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.
Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".
But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.
Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government" - remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.

item.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
item.description:
Image source, Villa Vie ResidencesImage caption,
The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into its voyage around the world when it came to a stop in CambodiaByKoh Ewe and Claire Graham, BBC News NIPublished28 October 2026, 03:05 GMTUpdated 10:31 GMT
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.
The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".
Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800.
Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.
There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.

item.title: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says
item.description:
Image source, Andrej ISAKOVIC / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Officers were visible outside the embassy in Belgrade later on Wednesday ByVicky WongPublished28 October 2026, 10:17 GMT
Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".
The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.
Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".
Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.
Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level – meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.
The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.
Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.
Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.
This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.
The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.
Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

item.title: Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
item.description:
Image source, Tanzania's energy ministryImage caption,
The energy minister described it as a "major milestone" for the East African nationByBasillioh RukangaPublished28 October 2026, 10:18 GMT
Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.
Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.
He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.
The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.
Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.
Image source, Tanzania's energy ministryImage caption,
Gas from the field will be for domestic and industrial power generation and also for vehicles
"The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.
Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.
In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.
Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.

item.title: Anger in Kenya over extradition hearing delay for ex-British soldier accused of murdering woman
item.description:
Image source, Rose WanyuaImage caption,
Agnes Wanjiru was discovered in a septic tank near a British army camp in Kenya in 2012 aged 21ByWycliffe Muia Reporting fromNairobiPublished28 October 2026, 08:28 GMT
The family of a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by a former British soldier 14 years ago has expressed outrage after being told an extradition hearing for the accused had been postponed until May 2027.
Relatives of Agnes Wanjiru, whose body was found in a septic tank near a British army training camp in Kenya in 2012, described the delay as "completely unacceptable" and have accused the authorities of failing to keep them informed.
Robert James Purkiss was arrested in the UK last November and is fighting extradition to Kenya to face trial for the murder of the 21-year-old mother.
He denies the allegation. His hearing was due to be held in London next month.
Murdered Kenyan's friends want UK soldier to face justice
Published21 September 2025
Wanjiru's niece, Esther Njoki, told the BBC that the family had learnt of the postponement through the UK embassy and had received no official explanation.
"We have exercised patience and endured uncertainty for years, but our patience is now being taken advantage of," she said in a statement.
"Agnes deserves justice. Her daughter Stacy deserves answers about what happened. And as a family, we deserve to be treated with dignity and kept informed about proceedings that profoundly affect our lives."
The family said it had already raised money and made arrangements to travel to the UK for the hearing, which was due to take place in three weeks.
It is now calling on the authorities to expedite the proceedings, warning that the latest postponement means the case will enter its 15th year without a trial.
The family said a UK court was expected next week to give the reasons for the hearing delay.

item.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
item.description:
Image source, Reuters/HandoutImage caption,
The people of Oleshky have had no electricity for years and no access to food or waterByPaul Kirby, Europe digital editor, Olga Malchevska and Dan Johnson, in KyivPublished27 October 2026
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.
Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.

item.title: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
King addresses 'suffering and injustices' in Bahamas pastByDaniela Relph, Royal correspondent, Reporting fromNassau and Henry MoorePublished27 October 2026Updated 28 October 2026 04:32 GMT
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.
Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.
His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.
The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.
Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.
Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.
King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.
The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.

item.title: Dutch zookeeper dies after being mauled by leopard
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandPublished27 October 2026
An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.
The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.
She sustained injuries to her head and neck and had emergency surgery, but the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.
An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.
Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.
"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.
The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.
Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injuries she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition.
A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.
"They are, and remain, predators."
Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.
